spans.text: Twenty minutes to six, and the gas ring in the kitchen went on with the small thump it made, and the boy in the front room heard it through the wall and did not move.

He had until a quarter past six. His mother would not come for him before then because the girls had to be got up first and washed at the sink one after the other, and that took what it took. His father had already gone. He had heard the door at ten to five, and the two flights of stairs, and then the street door, which stuck in warm weather and had to be pulled twice.

The flat at 1520 Lincoln Place had three rooms and a window on an airshaft. In September the airshaft still held the day before in it. He lay on his back with his hands behind his head and worked out the week again. Twelve dollars on Saturday. Ten of it went on the oilcloth by the sugar tin before he took his coat off, because that was how it was done and there had never been a conversation about it. Two dollars was his. Two dollars a week since April, less what he spent, which he kept honest with himself about, and the tin behind the Passover dishes on the high shelf had nine dollars and forty cents in it. Nobody looked behind the Passover dishes in September.

The place on Fulton Street wanted two dollars for the month and a dollar for gloves, and a boy could pay the two and use the house gloves, but the house gloves were wet the whole time and a man who did that would smell of other men's hands for a year. There was a photograph in the window of Benny Leonard with his arms down at his sides, which was the whole point of Benny Leonard, and underneath it a card in ink that said the terms.
His mother would want to know where nine dollars went.
At a quarter past six she came in and took the blanket off him in one movement, the way she did, and said his name once, and he was up.

Bread and tea standing at the sink. His sisters were still eating when he went, and the smaller one said something to him with her mouth full and he said something back. He put on his coat on the stairs. Out on Lincoln Place the sun was already over the roofs on the far side and it was going to be a warm one, the kind of September day that makes people say the summer is not done with yet.

He walked up to Utica Avenue with his hands in his pockets. The station there had been open three weeks and still smelled of wet cement, and the tile was so clean it looked wrong. He put his nickel in. Down the stairs, and the train came in and he got a seat, which he would not get after Nostrand, and then he did not get up when the woman with the parcels came on because he was sixteen and he was thinking about something else.

Under the river the lights went down and came back. Wall Street at eight minutes past eight. He came up into Broadway with about four hundred other people and went east and then south, and at Pine Street he ran the last block, because Blum and Sties had docked Kelly a quarter of a dollar in July for being four minutes late, and Kelly had said out loud in front of everybody that he did not care, and had gone very red saying it.
Eighty Pine. He was in the door at thirteen minutes past.
At forty-four Wall Street the brass was already half done.

John Johnson had let himself in at twenty-five past six with the watchman holding the grille for him, and the two of them had said what they said every morning, which was almost nothing and took about four seconds and neither would have known how to stop doing it. Then the watchman went off to sleep somewhere in Harlem and the lobby was his.

He had left West Eighty-fourth Street at twenty minutes to six. The express from Eighty-sixth at that hour carried men who did what he did and women who cleaned offices in the same buildings, and everybody sat and nobody talked, and at Times Square a great many of them got off and a great many more got on and by Chambers Street the car had gone quiet again.
Fifty-eight years old. Eleven of them in this lobby.

The work was the door plates first, then the long rail, then the elevator gates, then the four spittoons, which he did last because doing them first put you in a mood. Rottenstone and sweet oil on a rag for the plates. Whiting and a chamois after. You did not hurry the oil and you did not go at the corners with anything hard, and any man who told you different had never had to answer for a scratch in a piece of brass that four hundred people put their hands on in a day.

The marble was cold in the morning even in September. He worked on one knee with a folded sack under it and got up and moved the sack and went down again. His knees had opinions about the weather now and they were usually right two days ahead.

At half past seven the first clerks came through and he was on the elevator gates and did not look up, and one or two of them said good morning to him and the rest did not, and he had long ago stopped being able to remember which was which.

There was a trick to the gates that he had worked out in his second year and had never told anybody, because the man who had had the job before him had told him nothing at all and he had decided at the time that this was how the thing was passed on. You went along the bars in one direction only, all of them the same way, and the light came off them together. Go up one bar and down the next and you got a lobby full of brass that flickered when a man walked past it, and it looked like nothing on earth, and nobody could ever say why they did not like it.
By nine the lobby was full of men who owned the brass. It looked like water.

There was a bench by the mail desk where he took his coffee out of a can at half past ten, and from it he could see the whole floor, and on a Thursday morning in September the whole floor was moving. He knew the coats. He knew which of them belonged to men who would be in the building at seven that evening and which belonged to men who would be gone by three, and he had never once been wrong about a new man after the first week, and there was nobody he could have said this to who would have found it interesting.
In Jamaica the doctor had been twice and had used the word grippe both times, which Rudolf Portong had decided was the word doctors used when they meant they would come again on Friday.

He had the kettle on before he woke her. There was a way of doing it so the lid did not knock. He carried the cup in and set it on the chair by the bed because there was no table on that side, and she opened her eyes and looked at the cup and not at him.

Mrs. Enright was coming at nine and would stay until two. That was settled, it had been settled the night before and again at breakfast, and he said it once more anyway while he was getting into his coat, and she said she knew.

Twenty-five McAuley Avenue. He had been born eight streets and one railroad crossing from where he was standing, in Richmond Hill, and he had gone to the high school there and had come back to Queens after France with his hearing thick on one side, and now he counted other people's money in a marble room in Manhattan and lived four miles from his mother. It seemed to him a reasonable arrangement and it had never once occurred to him to say so out loud.
At the door he stopped with his hand on it.
I'll telephone at one,
he said.
She said something he did not catch. He said it again from the hall, one o'clock, and went down.

The seven twenty-nine out of Jamaica ran into Pennsylvania Station in twenty-two minutes when it was behaving. He had a paper and did not open it. At Thirty-fourth Street he went down and got the subway south with the rest of them, and he stood, and a man beside him was reading the racing page with his elbow in Portong's ribs the whole way, and Portong let him.

Fifty-five Wall by twenty past eight. There was a drawer to be counted before anybody could be served, and he counted it twice, because that was the kind of teller he was and the head of the cage knew it and it was the reason he had been moved up in March.
Carolyna Dickinson left the house on Hanover Street at twenty minutes to eight and walked to the Elmhurst station the long way, past where they were putting up the six new houses.

The long way was four minutes more. She had been taking it since June because the framing had gone up in June and she liked to see what they had done overnight, and there was a smell off the fresh lumber in the morning that she did not have a word for and did not need one for. Two of the six had roofs now. One had a bathtub standing on end in the front yard under a tarpaulin, which had been there eleven days.

Elmhurst still had corn in it. Not much, and not for long, and the men who came out on Sundays with the surveying rods had been coming out for two years, but there was a field behind the Bailey place with corn in it and it was standing brown and finished now and somebody would cut it and that would be that.

Forty-three years old. She had learned the machine in 1902, on a Remington with the type bars that struck up underneath so you could not see what you had written until you rolled it, and she had been faster on that machine than she was on the good one at Burr's, which was one of the very few things she had ever said out loud in an office and regretted.

She could take a hundred and forty words to the minute and hold it. There were two girls in the room who could take a hundred and forty for a burst. Nobody else in the room could hold it, and the men from the bond department who came in to dictate at that speed came to her desk and stood there and did it at her, and she wrote it, and one of them had told her once in front of the others that she was a marvel, and she had said thank you and gone on writing, because there was nothing else to say to a thing like that.
The train came. It was on time, which by the standards of the Long Island road in September was worth a remark, and a man in the seat behind her made it.
On Ridgewood Avenue, Marguerite Drury put the shoes in a paper bag and then took them out again and looked at them and put them back.

They were brown, with a strap and a low heel and a little stitched trim over the toe that you could not see from more than a yard off, which was the good part. Two dollars and ninety-five cents on Pitkin Avenue on Saturday afternoon, and the man had said they were a five and a half and she had made him bring the six, and he had been sour about it and had been wrong. She had walked twice up and down the shop and her sister had said they were fine, meaning that she wanted to go home.

She was not going to wear them until the weather turned. A new pair of shoes in this heat, on those pavements, with the tar going soft in the afternoon and the grit that came off the elevated, and by October they would be nothing. She had done that once, in 1913, with a pair of grey ones, and had never got over it.

But Miss Foley had asked what she had got, and she had said brown, and Miss Foley had made a face and said brown how, and there was no answering that in a hallway at half past five with your coat on. So the shoes went into a paper bag and the bag went under her arm with the other things, and the old black ones went on her feet.

Twenty-nine. Six years at Curtis, Mallet-Prevost and Colt, thirty Broadway, where half the correspondence went out in French and where she had learned to take French dictation in shorthand without understanding more than one word in five, which some of the men found funny and which she thought was a perfectly reasonable way to work. You wrote the sounds. You did not have to know what a thing meant to get it down right. She had told that to a clerk once and he had not believed her and had tested her on a paragraph, and she had given it back to him letter perfect, and he had said, well, and had not spoken to her much afterward.

Down Ridgewood to Fulton and up the iron stairs to the elevated. The steps had a give in them at the third landing that she had felt every working day for six years and that she assumed the railroad knew about and had decided was somebody else's problem.

The train came in with its noise and she got on. Over Fulton Street the morning went by underneath in pieces, awnings and the tops of wagons and a man on a ladder washing a window with the sun coming off it, and she held the paper bag on her lap with both hands so that nobody would put a knee against it.
Colin McClure had the eight-oh-four out of Yonkers and the same three men in it, and one of them was Farrell, who talked.

They went down along the river with the sun on the far bank, past the yards and the tank cars, and at Spuyten Duyvil somebody always said something about the water and today it was Farrell, and what he said was that it was flat as a floor, which it was. Farrell was in insurance and had a theory about the election, which he had told them nine times since Labor Day and would tell them again before the tunnel.

McClure was twenty-four. In the paper the next morning they would put the word banker after his name, which was the word for what he did if you needed one word, and which would have surprised the four men in his section who had watched him copy a run of foreign drafts by hand for two days in August because a machine had got the columns wrong and nobody trusted the machine after that.
At Ninety-sixth Street the light went out of the windows and the car got hot and stayed hot the whole way in, and Farrell got to the election.
Alfred Mayer was the last one out of the flat, which was normal, and he had heard about it, which was also normal.

Five hundred and eleven West One Hundred and Thirty-eighth. His mother, himself and his two brothers, and one bathroom, and a system that had taken four years to arrive at and that only failed when one of them got a girl. His brothers went out at ten past seven and twenty past. He went out at half past nine, because at Morton Trading a man of twenty-four who was called the manager could go out at half past nine, and because the cables from the other side did not begin to make sense until the middle of the morning anyway.
Beekman Street by twenty past ten. Two cables, one of them a mess and the mess not theirs. He wrote out the answer twice, tore up the first, and gave the second to the boy.
There was a man he had to see about a draft, and the man was on Wall Street, and the man had said come at half past twelve because he was no good before he had eaten.
Mayer put the thing in his inside pocket and looked at the clock and had two hours to fill and thought about nothing much.

He did not work in Wall Street. He had told his mother this twice in the last month, both times because she had said Wall Street when she meant downtown, and both times he had corrected her and both times she had said it again the following week. Beekman Street was Beekman Street. Wall Street was where you went when somebody who would not come to you had to be seen, and you went there four or five times a year, and you took the papers with you and you came back with them signed or you came back with them not signed.
He went out at eleven and walked, because the morning was too good to sit in.
At ten minutes to eleven a train came into the Wall Street station and stopped and stood there with its doors open longer than it needed to, and the people came off it and went up.

They came up in a body and broke apart at the top of the stairs the way they did, and by the time they were out on the pavement they were a hundred separate errands going in six directions. Men with folders under their arms. Two girls from a bond house with their hats new that week. A boy carrying a box tied with string and holding it out from his coat so the string would not mark it. An old man who stopped four steps from the top to get his breath and was gone round by everybody without a word, which he did not mind, because he had stopped there every working morning since the spring and had come to think of it as his.

Above them the sky was clear and going to stay clear. The chimes at Trinity had done nothing since ten o'clock and would do nothing until eleven. Down at the corner of Broad the traffic worked itself out the way it worked itself out every hour of every day, the drays and the motor trucks and a boy on a bicycle with his hand on the tailgate of a wagon, stealing a tow.

Along the north side of Wall a man was setting out a board with the day's cable rates chalked on it, and he got the last figure wrong and rubbed it out with his thumb and did it again, and nobody had seen it but a policeman, who said nothing. Two women went by carrying a rolled awning between them. A window went up on a second floor and stayed up.

The district in the middle of the morning was the loudest quiet place in America. It had a sound like a room full of people all doing arithmetic out loud, and everybody in it had been in it long enough to stop hearing it, and the only ones who ever remarked on it were visitors, who always said the same thing, and were always told the same thing back.
Four hundred people went up the stairs and into the day. Nothing happened to any of them.
The tally was out by two hundredths of an ounce and had been out since a quarter to eleven.

Two hundredths of a troy ounce is a thing you could lose in the sweat on a man's palm, and in the gold shipment department of J. P. Morgan and Company it was a morning. Joyce had the weight sheet on his left and the Assay Office receipt on his right and a pencil in his hand that he had not written anything with in six minutes, and he was going down the column for the third time with the flat of his thumbnail under each line.

The trouble with two hundredths was that it was too small to be a theft and too large to be nothing. A big discrepancy was almost always a copying error and it announced itself. A small one sat there and let you look at it.
Read me the fourth bar again,
he said.
Cusack read it. Joyce marked the sheet, and the mark did not help, and he put the pencil down.

Outside and below, the Assay Office was moving gold, and had been moving it since Monday, and would be at it until the end of the following week. It made a particular noise that you stopped hearing after about a year. There was the noise of the hand trucks on the sill plate, which was a knock and then a rumble, always in that order and always with the same pause between, so that you could count it. There was the noise of the boxes going down onto the boards. And there was, five or six times an hour, a shout from one man to another in the street, three words at most, the same three words, because a man carrying twenty-seven pounds of gold in a wooden box does not make conversation.

They said it was nine hundred millions of dollars altogether. It was probably not nine hundred millions. It was some number nobody in this building had the exact form of, and the sum of the guesses was that it was the largest quantity of the metal that had ever been moved across fifty feet of pavement anywhere on earth, and the men who were moving it were paid by the day and knocked off at twelve and did not come back until one.

Joyce had watched them go the day before. They shut the doors first. Then they stood on the step for a moment the way men do, and then they went off up toward Nassau in twos and threes, and one of them was eating something already.

There was a lesson in that transfer that he had tried twice to get across to younger men and had given up on. Everybody who came into this work arrived believing that the difficulty with gold was keeping people from stealing it. It was not. Almost nobody stole gold, for the same reason almost nobody stole a church organ: you could not get it away and you could not do anything with it once you had. The difficulty with gold was that it was heavy and soft and that every time a man put his hands on it the number attached to it had a chance to go wrong, and that once the number went wrong in the sixth place it stayed wrong through every book it entered for the rest of its life. The whole apparatus, the receipts, the countersignatures, the double weighing, the wax, the eleven initials on a manifest, existed to defeat arithmetic and not to defeat thieves. He had said this once at a dinner and had watched a man's face go politely blank.
He went down the column a fourth time.
At six minutes past eleven a boy came up from the cable room with three flimsies and Joyce read them standing.

The Saturday sailing was confirmed. Marine insurance was settled at the figure they had asked for and not the figure they had been offered on Tuesday, which meant that somebody in the London house had said something to somebody, and Joyce was pleased about it in the way a man is pleased about a thing he will never be told the details of. Sterling was where it had been, in the middle threes, which four years ago would have been news to sit down for and was now Thursday.

The third one was from Halifax and was about a case that had been opened and closed again on a pier in June, and it was the fourth cable on the subject, and every one of the four had said the same thing in slightly different words, which was that nothing was missing and nobody could say who had opened it. Joyce had a folder for that. It was getting thick. He would still be adding to it at Christmas and it would still say nothing at Christmas, and there was a species of man in this business who could not leave such a folder alone and would take it home, and Joyce was not one of them and had come to be quietly proud of not being one of them.
He signed two of the flimsies and gave them back to the boy and kept the third.
Tell Mr. Cusack I want the Wednesday sheet as well,
he said.
Not the copy. The one with the pencil on it.

The department occupied a long room with the windows on the Wall Street side, and eleven men worked in it, and it existed to do one thing, which was to see to it that when this firm undertook that a certain weight of gold would be in a certain vault or a certain ship's strongroom on a certain day, the gold was there, and the weight was right, and every hand it had passed through in between had signed for it. That was the whole of it. There was no cleverness in the work at all. There were men on the floor below who could make more money in an afternoon than his department handled in a year and could not have told you what a bar of it weighed.

Joyce was fifty-one and had been in the firm's employ for twenty-two years and had run this department for nine. He knew what he was worth to them and he knew, more precisely than most men are ever allowed to, the exact size and shape of the room he had come to the end of.

At a quarter past eleven a young man came up from the floor below with a query about a consignment for Rio that was not going to be a consignment for Rio and had never at any point been likely to be one, and Joyce dealt with him in under four minutes, which was two minutes longer than the thing was worth and two minutes shorter than the young man had expected, and sent him away with an answer he could take back downstairs and repeat as his own.
Then he stood at the window for perhaps twenty seconds and looked at nothing in particular.

The Assay Office men had a system for the boxes and it was a good one. Two on the truck, one at the sill, one on the step, and a fifth man with a book who touched nothing and stopped everything about every ninth box for reasons no observer could work out. Joyce had watched him for three days and had decided the man was going by the boxes and not by the clock, which meant he was counting a series in his head while doing something else, and Joyce had a certain respect for that.
At twenty past eleven his son came in.
William came in the way he came into everywhere, half a step too fast, with a folder under his arm that he had not been asked to bring up. He put it on the corner of the desk.
Mullaney says you wanted this yesterday.
I wanted it yesterday.
He says he sent it up yesterday.
He did not send it up yesterday.
That's what I told him.
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: William looked at the two sheets and the pencil and then, briefly, out of the window at the Assay Office, and then back.
You're on the fourth bar.
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: I am on the fourth bar for the fourth time.
It's the receipt,
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: William said.
It's always the receipt. They round the last figure over there when they're busy and then they don't.
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: Joyce did not say anything to that. It was very likely the answer, it was the answer he had been circling since eleven, and it was not the sort of thing a man wanted handed to him at twenty past by a person he had taught to ride a bicycle.

The boy was twenty-eight. He had gone over in the summer of 1918 with everybody else and had come back in the spring of 1919 with everybody else, thinner and taller and with a way of holding his head slightly to the right when somebody spoke to him from that side that he did not seem to know about. He had come into the firm in July of that year, into investment securities, which was two floors and one entire world away from a room full of weight sheets. Joyce had had nothing to do with it. He had said nothing to anybody about it, before or after, and had refused on principle to say to anybody afterward that he had said nothing, and the result was that every man in this building assumed he had done it, and there was no way of ever finding out whether they did or not.
Lunch,
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: William said.
Not today.
spans.speaker: Joyce

spans.text: It's Thursday.
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: It is Thursday and I have a sailing on Saturday and a receipt that is wrong and Mullaney owes me a sheet from yesterday.
spans.speaker: Joyce

spans.text: Tomorrow, then.
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: Tomorrow the shipment goes out.
spans.speaker: Joyce

spans.text: Then next Thursday,
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: William said,
and if you tell me next Thursday is anything I'll go and see Mother about it.
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: There was a standing arrangement about Thursdays. It was eleven years old. It had begun when the boy was at school and had come down to the district on a Thursday in the holidays because his mother had a thing she went to, and the two of them had eaten in a place on Nassau Street with sawdust on the floor, and it had somehow become a fixture, and like every fixture of that kind it survived on a rule that neither of them had ever stated: in a slow week you kept it and in a busy week you did not, and nobody minded, and if anybody had ever minded out loud the whole thing would have been finished inside a month.
This was a busy week.
How's the tailor,
spans.speaker: Joyce

spans.text: Joyce said.
The tailor is a thief.
The tailor is the same tailor I have gone to for nineteen years.
Then he has been robbing you for nineteen years and you have grown fond of him.
Joyce turned the receipt over, which told him nothing, because the back of a receipt tells nobody anything.

The wedding was a fortnight off. Two weeks and two days, in a church her people belonged to, and there would be a dinner afterward at which Joyce was expected to stand up and say something. He had known this since June. He had written four lines of it on the back of an envelope in August and had not looked at the envelope since, and it was in the left-hand drawer of the desk he was sitting at, under the blotting pads, and he was aware of it in the way a man is aware of a stone in his shoe when he is not walking.

The girl's name was the name of a girl he had met perhaps nine times, and he would have said, if anybody had asked, that she was sensible, which from him was a good deal. Her father was in wool. She had a laugh she did not seem able to get out quietly and had once got it out during a silence at his own table, and William had looked at her with an expression Joyce had recognised and had had to look away from.

What he had written in August, on the envelope, was that a father in this position is generally expected to say that he is losing a son, and that he had thought about it and had decided he was not going to say it, because it was not true and because everybody in the room would know it was not true. Then there were three more lines that did not go anywhere. He had put the pen down and had not picked it up again in five weeks, and he had a fortnight, and he was not worried about it, and he thought about it perhaps twice a day.
Hennessy's coming,
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: William said.
I heard yesterday.
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: Joyce looked up.
From Pittsburgh?
From Pittsburgh. He's bringing the wife.

There had been four of them who went out together from the block in 1918 and three who came back, and Hennessy was one of the three and had gone to Pittsburgh in 1919 and had not been east since. Joyce had known his mother for twenty years. He put that away carefully where he could get at it later and said only that they would have to do something about the table, and William said that his mother had already done something about the table, on Sunday, and had not mentioned it to either of them.
She doesn't tell me anything,
spans.speaker: Joyce

spans.text: Joyce said.
She tells you everything. You're reading a weight sheet.
I'll want you for an hour on Saturday about the flat,
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: William said.
Not the whole day. An hour.
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: Saturday.
spans.speaker: Joyce

spans.text: An hour.
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: Ask your mother about Saturday.
spans.speaker: Joyce

spans.text: I asked her Sunday and she said ask you.
spans.speaker: William

spans.text: Then it is settled,
spans.speaker: Joyce

spans.text: Joyce said,
and neither of us will find out how until Saturday morning.
spans.speaker: Joyce

spans.text: William laughed and went to the door and stopped there, and said,
"It is the receipt, you know,"
and went out.

Joyce sat for a moment and then got up and went along to Cusack's desk and told him to send a man over to the Assay Office and ask them to read back the fourth entry off their own book. Cusack said the Assay Office would not care for that. Joyce said that the Assay Office had been not caring for it since 1908 and had never once refused.
He came back and took the Wednesday sheet, which had arrived, and put it beside the other two.

There was a way the light came into that room in the late morning in September, off the stone across the street, which made everything on a desk about a shade too bright to read for about twenty minutes, and every man in the department dealt with it his own way. Joyce moved the sheets six inches to the left.

He had a note to write to a man in Ottawa. He wrote it. He had the Saturday manifest to initial in eleven places and he initialled it in eleven places, and at the ninth he thought about the fourth bar again and was fairly sure by then that the boy was right, which was a thing that had started happening about two years ago and had not yet stopped being remarkable.

The man he had sent over came back at half past eleven and said the Assay Office would read the entry after one o'clock and not before, because the clerk who kept that book was on the transfer this week and could not be got at, and Joyce said that was fine, and it was fine, and he wrote a line on the corner of the receipt so that he would not have to hold it in his head over lunch.

Two of the younger men in the room were arguing quietly about the Yankees, who had been in the thing until a week ago and were now three back with a fortnight to go, and one of them said Cleveland and the other one said not with that pitching, and Joyce, who did not follow it, could have told either of them the standing, because he had heard the argument every morning since the middle of August and it never changed except in the numbers.

At about a quarter to twelve the knock and rumble from below changed. They were on the last run before they shut. There would be four or five more boxes and then the doors and then the step and then Nassau Street.
At ten minutes to twelve Cusack said something about a man from the Guaranty who had been waiting since half past, and Joyce put the manifest in the drawer on top of the envelope and went down.

On the stairs he came up behind a knot of men going the same way and had to take it at their pace, which he did not mind. In the hall below they broke left toward the street and he saw his son among them, hatless, because it was that kind of day, and one of the others said something and all three of them looked out at the light before they went through the door.

Joyce turned the other way, into the small room off the hall, where the man from the Guaranty had been sitting for twenty minutes with his hat on his knee and was going to want an explanation. That took a while. Then there would be the Assay Office and their fourth entry, and after that the Wednesday sheet, and it was going to be two o'clock before he got anything to eat and he had known that since nine in the morning.
He put his hand out to the man from the Guaranty and apologised for the wait.
